grammar.title: Question forms
points: Yes/No questions in simple tenses need do, does or did + infinitive: Does Marta cycle to school? Did you lock the door?
With be, continuous and perfect tenses and modal verbs, put the auxiliary before the subject: Is he ready? Have they left? Can you swim?
Wh- questions use the same order after the question word: Where does your cousin live? Why were you laughing?
Object questions (asking about the object) need an auxiliary: What did Leo break? (He broke a glass.)
Subject questions (who/what is the subject) keep statement order, with no do/does/did: Who broke the glass? NOT Who did break the glass?
questions: ____ your sister play the guitar? (Do / Does / Is) | Does
Where ____ you go last weekend? (do / did / were) | did
Correct it: Who did phone you last night? | Who phoned you last night?

____ you ever eaten sushi? (Did / Have / Are) | Have
Correct it: Why you are late? | Why are you late?
Make a question: She can speak Italian. ____ Italian? | Can she speak

grammar.title: Present tense review
points: Present simple for habits, routines, permanent situations and facts: My dad works in a bank. Water freezes at 0 degrees.
Present continuous for things happening now, temporary situations and fixed future plans: I'm staying with my aunt this week. We're meeting Sam at six.
State verbs (know, like, want, believe, understand, need, belong) are not normally used in continuous forms: I know the answer, NOT I'm knowing the answer.
Some verbs change meaning: I think it's great (opinion) / I'm thinking about lunch (mental activity); She has a dog / She's having a shower.
Present perfect + for (a period) or since (a starting point) for situations that began in the past and continue now: We've had this car for six years / since 2019.

Be quiet! The baby ____ (sleep). | is sleeping

grammar.title: Past tense review
points: Past simple for finished actions and past states: We moved here in 2019. I didn't like vegetables as a child.
Past continuous (was/were + -ing) for an action in progress at a past moment, or as background: At nine I was walking the dog.
A longer action (past continuous) is often interrupted by a shorter one (past simple): I was having a shower when the phone rang.
Past perfect (had + past participle) shows that one past action happened before another: When we arrived, the film had already started.
used to + infinitive for past habits or states that are no longer true; negatives and questions use 'use to': I used to hate tomatoes. Did you use to live here?

grammar.title: Making comparisons
points: Use comparative + than, or less + adjective + than: Trains are faster than buses. This phone is less expensive than that one.
as + adjective + as means equal; not as/so ... as means less: Leo is as tall as his dad. My room isn't as big as yours.
the + comparative, the + comparative shows that two things change together: The more you practise, the better you play.
Make a comparative stronger or weaker with far, a lot, a great deal / a bit, a little, slightly: far more interesting, slightly cheaper.
Make superlatives stronger with by far or easily: It's by far the best pizza in town.

grammar.title: Relative clauses
points: Defining relative clauses say which person or thing we mean, with no commas: The girl who sits next to me is from Peru.
Use who/that for people, which/that for things, whose for possession, where for places and when for times.
You can leave out who, which or that when it is the object of the clause: The film (that) we saw was brilliant. But not when it is the subject: The boy who won is my cousin.
Non-defining relative clauses add extra information between commas: My grandad, who is 80, still plays tennis.
In non-defining clauses you cannot use that and you cannot leave out the pronoun: This phone, which I bought last week, is already broken.

This is the café ____ we had breakfast. (which / where / when) | where

grammar.title: Present perfect and past simple
points: Present perfect (have/has + past participle) links past and present: for situations that started in the past and continue, and for past events when the time isn't given: I've lost my keys.
Use it for things repeated in a period up to now: She's phoned three times this morning.
Typical words: just (a moment ago), already (sooner than expected), yet (at the end of questions and negatives), still (+ negative), ever, never: I still haven't finished. Have you eaten yet?
Past simple for finished actions at a finished time (yesterday, last week, in 2020, two days ago): I lost my keys yesterday.
Don't use the present perfect with a finished time expression: NOT I've seen him yesterday.

grammar.title: Modals of ability and possibility and managed to
points: Present ability: can / can't or am/is/are able to: I can swim but I can't dive.
General ability in the past: could / couldn't or was/were able to: My gran could speak three languages.
For success on one specific occasion in the past use managed to or was/were able to, NOT could: The door was stuck, but we managed to open it. (couldn't is fine in the negative.)
can has no future or perfect forms, so use be able to: I'll be able to drive next year. I haven't been able to sleep.
may/might be able to for a possible future ability: I might be able to come on Friday.

grammar.title: Future (1): plans and intentions
points: Present simple for timetables and fixed schedules: The museum opens at ten tomorrow. School starts on 9 September.

Adverbs like definitely and probably go after will but before won't, and after be with going to: I'll probably go. I probably won't go. She's definitely going to win.

grammar.title: The passive
points: Form: the right tense of be + past participle: Coffee is grown in Brazil. The bridge was built in 1900. The hall is being cleaned. My bike has been stolen.
Use the passive when we don't know or don't care who does the action, or when the action or object is more important.
Add by + agent only when it is important to say who did it: This song was written by a teenager.
With modals: modal + be + past participle: Phones must be switched off. The match might be cancelled.
The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive: They make cheese here -> Cheese is made here.

grammar.title: Present perfect continuous
points: Form: have/has been + -ing: I've been waiting. She hasn't been sleeping well. Have you been crying?
Use it for an activity that started in the past and is still going on or has just stopped, often with a visible result: You're all wet! - I've been washing the car.
Use it with for, since and how long to stress how long an activity has lasted: We've been playing for two hours.
The present perfect simple focuses on the finished result or on how many/how much: I've written three emails. Compare: I've been writing emails all morning.
State verbs (know, be, have = own, like, believe) take the simple form: I've known her for years, NOT I've been knowing her.

grammar.title: Zero and first conditionals
points: Zero conditional: if + present, present, for things that are always or generally true; here if means almost the same as when: If you heat ice, it melts.
First conditional: if + present, will + infinitive, for a real possibility in the future and its result: If it rains, we'll stay in.
Never use will in the if-clause: If I see her (NOT will see), I'll tell her.
The if-clause can come first (with a comma) or second (no comma): We'll stay in if it rains.
Use may, might or could instead of will when the result is less certain: If we leave now, we might catch the bus.
In the first conditional, if = perhaps it will happen; when = it certainly will: When I get home, I'll call you.

grammar.title: Reported statements
points: When the reporting verb is past (said, told), the tense usually moves one step back: present -> past, past simple and present perfect -> past perfect: 'I'm tired' -> She said she was tired.
will -> would, can -> could, may -> might, must -> had to, am going to -> was going to. could, would, should, might and the past perfect don't change.
Pronouns and time/place words change: I -> he/she, my -> his/her, today -> that day, tomorrow -> the next day, yesterday -> the day before, here -> there.
say (something) but tell + person: He said (that) he was late. He told me (that) he was late.
If something is still true or is a permanent fact, the tense can stay the same: She said the Earth goes round the Sun.
questions: 'I like pizza.' -> He said he ____ pizza. | liked
'We are leaving.' -> They said they ____ leaving. | were
'I will help you.' -> She said she ____ help me. | would
'I can't swim.' -> He said he ____ swim. | couldn't
He ____ me that he was tired. (said / told) | told
'I saw Ana yesterday.' -> He said he had seen Ana ____. (the day before / the next day / that day) | the day before
'I've finished.' -> She said she ____ finished. | had
'We must go.' -> They said they ____ go. | had to
'I'll call you tomorrow.' -> She said she'd call me ____. (the day before / the next day / that day) | the next day
She ____ that she was busy. (said / told) | said
'I'm going to win.' -> He said he ____ going to win. | was
'I live here.' -> She said she lived ____. (here / there / that) | there

grammar.title: Reported questions; reported requests
points: Tenses, pronouns and time words change just as in reported statements: 'Where do you live?' -> He asked where I lived.
Word order is like a statement (subject before verb) and there is no question mark: He asked where the bank was, NOT where was the bank.
Don't use do, does or did in reported questions: 'Why did you leave?' -> She asked why I had left.
Wh- questions keep the question word; Yes/No questions use if or whether: He asked if I liked football.
ask can be followed by an object: They asked us where we were going.
Report requests with ask + person + (not) to + infinitive: 'Please sit down' -> She asked me to sit down. 'Don't shout' -> He asked us not to shout.
questions: 'Where do you live?' -> She asked me where I ____. | lived
'Are you hungry?' -> He asked ____ I was hungry. (if / that / what) | if
Correct it: She asked where was the station. | She asked where the station was.
'Can you help me?' -> He asked me ____ help him. (to / if / that) | to
'Please don't be late.' -> She asked us ____ late. | not to be
'How old is he?' -> She asked how old ____. | he was
'Did you see the match?' -> She asked if I ____ the match. | had seen
Correct it: He asked me what did I want. | He asked me what I wanted.
'Will you come?' -> They asked whether I ____ come. | would
'Open the window, please.' -> She asked me ____ the window. | to open
'Why are you crying?' -> He asked her why she ____. | was crying
'Have you finished?' -> The teacher asked if we ____. | had finished

grammar.title: Have/get something done; get someone to do something
points: have/get + object + past participle = another person (usually a professional) does the job for you: I had my watch repaired. She's getting her nails done.
get is more informal than have; both can be used in any tense: We're going to have the kitchen painted.
Add by + person only if it matters who did it: I had my portrait painted by a street artist.
have something done can also describe something bad that happened to you: He had his phone stolen on the metro.
get + person + to + infinitive = ask or persuade somebody to do something: I got my brother to help me with the maths.
Compare: I painted my room (I did it) / I had my room painted (someone else did it).
questions: I ____ my teeth checked yesterday. (had / did / made) | had
She's going to get her ears ____ (pierce). | pierced
We got the waiter ____ (take) a photo of us. | to take
Put in order: had / I / fixed / my phone | I had my phone fixed
He ____ his wallet stolen on the bus. (had / made / did) | had
My parents are having the house ____ (paint) this week. | painted
I'll get my dad ____ (drive) us to the station. | to drive
Who painted it? 'Eva had her room painted.' (Eva / someone else) | someone else
You should ____ your eyes tested. (get / make / do) | get
Correct it: I got Ana help me. | I got Ana to help me.
We ____ (have) our car washed every month. | have
Did you ____ your photo taken for the passport? (have / make / be) | have

grammar.title: Second conditional
points: Form: if + past simple, would + infinitive (or the other way round, without a comma): If I had more time, I'd learn Chinese.
Use it for imaginary or unlikely situations in the present or future: If I won the lottery, I'd buy a boat.
might instead of would makes the result less certain; could = would be able to: If you asked her, she might say yes.
After if, I/he/she/it can take were instead of was, especially to give advice: If I were you, I'd say sorry.
wish / if only + past simple = you want a present situation to be different: I wish I had a dog. If only I were taller!
wish / if only + would for things you want to change, often when you are annoyed; + could for abilities: I wish you would listen! I wish I could fly.
questions: If I ____ (have) a car, I'd drive to school. | had
If she studied more, she ____ (pass) the exam. | would pass
If I ____ you, I'd apologise. (were / am / be) | were
Correct it: If I would have time, I'd help. | If I had time, I'd help.
I wish I ____ (know) the answer, but I don't. | knew
If only we ____ (not / have) an exam tomorrow! | didn't have
I wish you ____ stop making that noise! (would / will / did) | would
What ____ (you / do) if you found a wallet? | would you do
If we lived by the sea, we ____ go surfing, but I'm not sure. (might / will / can) | might
I wish I ____ play the piano. (could / can / would to) | could
He ____ (not / be) so tired if he went to bed earlier. | wouldn't be
Real or imaginary? 'If I had wings, I'd fly.' (real / imaginary) | imaginary

grammar.title: Modals of deduction: present
points: Use modal + infinitive to say how sure you are about a present situation.
must = I'm almost sure it's true: She must be tired; she's been working all day.
can't = I'm almost sure it's NOT true (don't use mustn't for this): That can't be Tom; he's in Paris.
may, might, could = it's possible; add well (may well, might well) when it's quite probable: He might be at the gym. It may well rain.
may not / might not = perhaps not. could not is not used with this meaning.
For something happening right now use modal + be + -ing: They must be having lunch.
questions: She's yawning. She ____ be tired. (must / can't / mustn't) | must
That ____ be Dan; Dan is much taller. (must / can't / might) | can't
I'm not sure where Eva is. She ____ be in the library. (might / must / can't) | might
Correct it: It mustn't be true! | It can't be true!
The lights are on, so someone ____ be at home. (must / can't / might not) | must
It's only a guess, but this ____ be the right street. (could / must / can't) | could
You've just had lunch! You ____ be hungry again! (can't / must / may) | can't
Don't phone now; they might ____ (have) dinner. | be having
He ____ not know the answer; ask someone else. (might / must / could) | might
How sure? 'It must be broken.' (almost sure / just possible) | almost sure
Her French is perfect. She ____ have French parents. (may well / can't / mustn't) | may well
Which means 'perhaps not'? (might not / can't) | might not

grammar.title: Third conditional
points: Form: if + past perfect, would have + past participle: If I'd seen you, I would have said hello.
Use it for imaginary situations in the past (things that did not happen) and their imagined results: If we'd left earlier, we wouldn't have missed the train. (We left late and missed it.)
might have = the result was only possible; could have = would have been able to: If you'd asked, I might have helped.
'd can be had (in the if-clause) or would (in the result): If I'd known, I'd have come.
wish / if only + past perfect expresses regret about the past: I wish I had studied more. If only I hadn't said that!
Don't use would have in the if-clause: NOT If I would have known.
questions: If I ____ (know) about the party, I'd have gone. | had known
If she had run faster, she ____ (win) the race. | would have won
If I ____ seen him, I'd have waved. (had / would have / have) | had
I wish I ____ (not / eat) so much cake last night. | hadn't eaten
We ____ (not / get) lost if we'd taken a map. | wouldn't have got
If only I ____ (bring) my umbrella this morning! | had brought
'If it had rained, we'd have stayed home.' Did it rain? (yes / no) | no
If you'd told me, I ____ have helped, but I'm not certain. (might / will / can) | might
In 'If I'd known', 'd = ____. (had / would) | had
In 'I'd have called', 'd = ____. (had / would) | would
What ____ (you / do) if you had missed the flight? | would you have done
She wishes she ____ (study) harder for last week's test. | had studied

grammar.title: Modals of deduction: past
points: Use modal + have + past participle to make guesses about the past.
must have = I'm almost sure it happened: The grass is wet; it must have rained.
can't have / couldn't have = I'm almost sure it didn't happen: She can't have left; her coat is still here.
may have, might have, could have = perhaps it happened: He might have missed the bus.
may not have / might not have = perhaps it didn't happen: They might not have seen your message.
have never changes to has or had after a modal: She must have forgotten, NOT must has forgotten.
questions: The street is wet. It ____ have rained. (must / can't / might not) | must
He ____ have stolen it; he was with me all day. (can't / must / may) | can't
I'm not sure why she's late. She ____ have missed the bus. (might / must / can't) | might
Correct it: She must has forgotten. | She must have forgotten.
They must have ____ (go) out; nobody's answering. | gone
You ____ have seen Leo in town; he's in Peru! (can't / must / might) | can't
He didn't reply. He ____ not have seen my text. (might / must / can) | might
She got 10 in the exam. She ____ have studied a lot. (must / can't / might not) | must
Where are my keys? I could have ____ (leave) them at school. | left
How sure? 'He may have called.' (almost sure / just possible) | just possible
Correct it: They can't had finished already. | They can't have finished already.
The window is broken. Someone ____ (must / break) it. | must have broken

grammar.title: -ing forms
points: The -ing form can be the subject or object of a sentence: Swimming is great exercise. I've finished tidying my room.
Use -ing after verbs of liking and disliking (love, enjoy, hate, can't stand, don't mind): I can't stand queuing.
Always use -ing after a preposition, including adjective + preposition: She's good at drawing. I'm tired of waiting. He left without saying goodbye.
An -ing participle clause can add information or replace a second sentence: I saw Tom waiting outside the cinema. Feeling tired, I went to bed early.
It can show two actions happening at the same time, and the negative is not + -ing: Not knowing the way, we asked a police officer.
The subject of the participle clause must be the same as the subject of the main verb: Cycling to school, I saw a fox. (= I was cycling.)
questions: ____ (eat) too much sugar is bad for you. | Eating
I'm interested in ____ (learn) Japanese. | learning
She's really good at ____ (dance). | dancing
Correct it: He left without to say goodbye. | He left without saying goodbye.
Do you enjoy ____ (play) board games? | playing
____ (not / want) to be late, I took a taxi. | Not wanting
____ (feel) hungry, we stopped for a sandwich. | Feeling
I saw a man ____ (climb) through the window. | climbing
Correct it: I'm afraid of fly. | I'm afraid of flying.
Who was walking? 'Walking to school, Ana found a coin.' (Ana / the coin) | Ana
Thank you for ____ (help) me with my project. | helping
I don't mind ____ (wait) a few minutes. | waiting
